name: Ultimate attribution error
statement: Prejudiced observers explain a bad act by an outgroup member as the group's nature, and explain the same person's good act away as luck or an exception.
meaning: Pettigrew's proposal has two halves that point in opposite directions. A negative act by an outgroup member is read as disposition, in his wording often as genetically determined. A positive act by the same person is read as the exceptional case, as luck or special advantage, as unusual motivation and effort, or as a situation that forced the act. That second half is what separates the idea from the fundamental attribution error, which predicts a dispositional reading whatever the behaviour is. It also differs from in-group favouritism in what gets counted. Favouritism is measured in what people hand over, in money or cooperation; this is measured in the causes they name. Pettigrew put prejudice in the antecedent, writing that prejudiced people do this more than others, so the claim covers a subset of observers rather than everyone.

origin.note: The paper extends the cognitive chapters of Allport's The Nature of Prejudice with attribution theory, proposes the error in two numbered predictions, and says which of the four ways of discounting a positive outgroup act will be chosen and when the phenomenon will be magnified. Only its abstract at Crossref was read for this entry. The empirical case it draws on came five years earlier, from Taylor and Jaggi in southern India.

evidence: Taylor and Jaggi asked Hindu participants to explain the behaviour of Hindu and Muslim actors performing socially desirable and socially undesirable acts, scoring internal against external causes. Their abstract reports internal attributions for ingroup actors doing desirable things and external attributions for ingroup actors doing undesirable things, with the converse for the same acts by Muslims. The article is paywalled, so no means, cell sizes or test statistics from it appear on this page. Hewstone reviewed the literature eleven years after Pettigrew named the error. His abstract counts 19 studies across three paradigms, explanations for positive and negative outcomes, explanations for success and failure, and explanations for group differences, and says the ingroup-favouring tendency appears in most of them. It also says the evidence gives only limited support to Pettigrew's error, and that in any given study the bias is confined to particular dimensions. The three findings he calls strongest are more internal attribution for ingroup positive acts and less for ingroup negative acts, more attribution of outgroup failure to lack of ability alongside explaining outgroup success away as luck or effort or an easy task, and a preference for ingroup-serving accounts of group differences.

replication.headline: Pettigrew's two predictions come apart under direct test. The positive-behaviour half survives, the negative-behaviour half does not, and one Delhi study was corrected to report no bias at all.
replication.detail: Khan and Liu tested both predictions with hypothetical scenarios among 148 Indians, 91 Hindu and 57 Muslim, and 145 Pakistanis, 107 Muslim and 38 Hindu. Their abstract reports that the first prediction, dispositional attribution of negative outgroup behaviour, received little support, and that the second, situational attribution of positive outgroup behaviour, received considerable but not total support. They call the overall result mixed and describe the pattern as ingroup favouring more than outgroup derogating. Khandelwal, Dhillon, Akalamkam and Papneja compared 321 Muslim adolescents, 239 male and 82 female, in Kashmir and in Delhi. The Kashmiri group made more ethnocentric attributions for ingroup positive behaviour, with no difference between the two samples on negative behaviour. Misra and Mishra ran 95 university students in Delhi, 51 from the General Caste category and 44 from the Scheduled Caste category, on success and failure scenarios scored for locus of causality, stability and controllability. The abstract as published reports no intergroup attribution bias in the General Caste group and ingroup derogation in the Scheduled Caste group. A correction in the next issue rewrites that abstract to say both groups showed no intergroup attribution bias, and points to social desirability as something the finding leaves to be investigated. Priedols, Dimdins, Gaina, Leja and Austers gave 222 Latvian students a policy initiative from a trusted or a distrusted party. Dispositional explanations moved as Pettigrew predicted, with success credited to a trusted party's benevolence, competence and integrity and failure blamed on a distrusted party's lack of them. Explanations by external circumstances showed no sign of the error. The largest effects in this area come from a design that is not Pettigrew's. Zell, Stockus and Bernstein asked American partisans how far Republican and Democratic policies had caused eight positive and 12 negative national outcomes, rated from 1 to 7. In Study 1, 244 MTurk workers in July 2016, the party by positive-credit by negative-blame interaction ran at F(1, 242) = 288.25, p < .001, partial eta squared .54. A summary bias index differed from zero at d = 1.21 among the 163 Democrats and d = 1.14 among the 81 Republicans. The preregistered Study 2, 249 registered voters in July 2020, gave F(1, 247) = 151.55, p < .001, partial eta squared .38, with the index at d = 0.85 among 135 Democrats and d = 0.73 among 114 Republicans. The two parties did not differ in either study, p = .134 and p = .288. What that measures is how much responsibility for an outcome each group is assigned, not whether one act gets an internal or an external cause.

study.cite: Khan, S. S., & Liu, J. H. (2008). Intergroup attributions and ethnocentrism in the Indian subcontinent: The ultimate attribution error revisited. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 39(1), 16-36.

limits: No effect size for the ultimate attribution error is quoted on this page, because none was obtained from a source that could be opened. Pettigrew's 1979 paper, Hewstone's 1990 review, Taylor and Jaggi's 1974 study and the Khan and Liu, Khandelwal and Priedols articles were all reached only as abstracts, at Crossref or at the publisher's article page, and abstracts do not carry cell means or test statistics. That is why the structured fields above are empty and why the Zell figures, which come from a full text, sit in the prose with their design stated. No meta-analysis of intergroup causal attribution was located. The search covered Crossref by title and by bibliographic query, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, CORE and general web search, and turned up Hewstone's narrative review of 19 studies with no pooled estimate in its abstract. The Misra and Mishra article page still shows the uncorrected abstract, so a reader who stops there gets ingroup derogation where the correction gives no bias. Every direct test read here used hypothetical scenarios or written vignettes rather than observed behaviour, and all of them are single samples from India, Pakistan, Kashmir or Latvia.
misreadings: The commonest reading treats this as the fundamental attribution error with a group swapped in for a person. It is not that. The fundamental attribution error predicts a dispositional reading of behaviour in general, while Pettigrew's second prediction is that a good act by an outgroup member gets a situational reading, which is the opposite direction. The half that keeps failing is the dispositional half, so the part of the idea that looks most like the fundamental attribution error is the part with the least support behind it. A second reading collapses it into in-group favouritism. Favouritism is counted in allocations and cooperation between groups; this is a claim about the causes people give for one act, and the two can move apart. A third drops Pettigrew's condition. His abstract restricts both predictions to prejudiced people and says they will do this more than others, which makes prejudice a moderator rather than the effect being universal. The clause about attributing outgroup faults to genetics belongs to the original statement and is usually dropped in retelling. Zell and colleagues add a caution that applies to the whole family: a group-favouring attribution is a bias in the statistical sense, and bias in that sense does not by itself mean the attribution is wrong.

sources.text: Pettigrew, T. F. (1979). The ultimate attribution error: Extending Allport's cognitive analysis of prejudice. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 5(4), 461-476. Read as its abstract at Crossref; the full text was not reached.

Taylor, D. M., & Jaggi, V. (1974). Ethnocentrism and causal attribution in a South Indian context. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 5(2), 162-171. Paywalled; described here from its abstract at Crossref, and no figure on this page comes from it.

Hewstone, M. (1990). The 'ultimate attribution error'? A review of the literature on intergroup causal attribution. European Journal of Social Psychology, 20(4), 311-335. Paywalled; the count of 19 studies and the verdict of limited support are read from its abstract at Crossref.

Khan, S. S., & Liu, J. H. (2008). Intergroup attributions and ethnocentrism in the Indian subcontinent: The ultimate attribution error revisited. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 39(1), 16-36. Described from its abstract at Crossref.

Khandelwal, K., Dhillon, M., Akalamkam, K., & Papneja, D. (2014). The ultimate attribution error: Does it transcend conflict? The case of Muslim adolescents in Kashmir and Delhi. Psychological Studies, 59(4), 427-435. Described from the abstract on the publisher's article page.

Misra, S., & Mishra, A. K. (2020). Is ultimate attribution error universal? Inter-group attribution for success and failure among university students in Delhi. Psychological Studies, 65(1), 64-73. The abstract on the publisher's page reports ingroup derogation in the Scheduled Caste group; see the correction below.

Psychological Studies, 65(1), 74-75. Rewrites the abstract and discussion to say both caste groups showed no inter-group attribution bias.
